name: Tembeta

lead: The tembeta is a rod or plug set in a piercing beneath the lower lip, traditionally by Guarani, Tupi and related peoples of South America. It is face adornment in the most literal sense: a polished stone, resin or wooden piece that sits in the lip and changes the look of the lower face.

In the cultures that wear it, it also signals the passage from boyhood to manhood and is believed to protect the mouth. Archaeologists have recovered tembetas of stone and resin that date back well over a thousand years, and clinical studies have recorded what long-term wear does to the teeth and jaw.

paras: A piercing is made in the lower lip, historically at initiation, and the opening holds a rod, often T-shaped, with a flange resting inside the mouth against the gums. Pieces were carved from quartz or other stone, wood or resin. In modern body-modification, the equivalent is a labret stud or plug in a lip piercing.

Studies of lip-plug wearers describe tooth displacement, jaw changes and heavy tooth wear, and case reports describe carcinoma arising at the plug site in a small number of wearers. Piercings can also become infected.

angle.text: The tembeta changes the appearance of the lower face directly while worn, and in its home cultures marks adulthood. Its look and meaning are tied to Indigenous tradition.

lead: The tembeta (also tembetá) is a lip ornament, a rod worn in a hole pierced beneath the lower lip by several Indigenous South American peoples, including the Guarani, Tupi and Chiriguano [1]. It is both decoration, shaping how the lower face looks, and a marker of belonging and maturity.

Tembetas were made of stone, often quartz, and of wood and resin; Guarani examples are described as T-shaped quartz about 10 cm long [1]. The practice is attested archaeologically across Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina and Chile, with a rare resin tembeta from Brazil dated to about 1,600 years ago examined by Raman spectroscopy [2].
Medical and anthropological studies of lip plugs in several cultures document effects on teeth and jaws and rare cases of cancer at the plug site [3][4][5][6].
infobox: Quartz and other stone, wood, resin [1][2]

paras: Descriptions of the tembeta emphasize initiation: a young man received the lip piercing at the ceremony marking entry into adulthood, after which he could marry [1]. Wearers regarded it as protecting the mouth, seen as a point of vulnerability, against harmful forces [1]. Some pipe-shaped versions of talc may have been used to smoke herbs in rites [1].
Lip ornaments occur widely, from Northwest Coast labrets of status to the Aztec tentetl, and meanings vary with each culture [7].

Early studies placed the origin of the tembeta in the Brazilian Planalto, with use spreading south to coastal Chile [1]. El Molle tembetas in Chile were curved plates fitted to the gums with a central button passing through the lip [1]. A 2004 analysis of a Brazilian resin tembeta, about 1,600 years old, found triterpenoid-rich material resembling Pistacia resin [2].

Studies of lip-plug wearers, not of tembetas specifically, describe effects of long-term wear. In Brazilian Zoe Indians, a study using jaw models found that lip plugs shift tooth position and jaw growth, with palatal displacement of upper lateral incisors, mandibular retraction depending on plug size, and tooth abrasion, the changes scaling with years of wear [3]. Among Makonde people in Tanzania, case series documented oral and dental damage from lip plugs called ndonya [4]. Case reports from Tanzania describe carcinoma of the upper lip associated with a lip plug, treated by excision with an Abbe flap [5], and a 1974 paper discussed the causes of lip plug carcinoma and its geographic distribution [6].
